name: New Horizons
intro: New Horizons made the first flyby of Pluto in July 2015, then visited Arrokoth, the most distant world ever explored up close. It is still working, cruising through the icy Kuiper Belt about 66 times farther from the Sun than Earth.
whyLeft: It has not been left: it is still working. But it is flying too fast to ever stop, so it will leave the solar system and never come back.
repurpose: It already reuses its own time well: it sleeps for long stretches to save energy, then wakes to study the Kuiper Belt and the space around it.

hotspots.title: The dish home
hotspots.text: This 2.1-meter dish sends data home so slowly that the Pluto pictures took about 16 months to arrive. Its messages now take about 9 hours to reach Earth.

hotspots.title: The Pluto camera
hotspots.text: A telescope camera called LORRI watched Pluto grow from a dot into a world with mountains of ice and a giant heart-shaped plain, during the flyby on 14 July 2015.

video.caption: A flight over Pluto made from New Horizons’ sharpest real pictures: the heart-shaped plain, then craters and icy mountains. No sound.

hotspots.title: Nuclear power
hotspots.text: Sunlight is far too weak out here for solar panels, so a nuclear generator on this side makes New Horizons’ electricity. It gives a little less power every year.

hotspots.title: The students’ dust counter
hotspots.text: University students built an instrument that counts specks of dust hitting the spacecraft. It is named after Venetia Burney, who suggested the name Pluto when she was 11.

hotspots.title: A special passenger
hotspots.text: A small container on New Horizons holds some of the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh, the astronomer who discovered Pluto in 1930. He finally got to visit it.

hotspots.title: Long naps
hotspots.text: To save energy, New Horizons spends long stretches asleep. In June 2026 it woke up healthy from its longest nap yet, more than 10 months.

source.label: NASA: New Horizons wakes from hibernation (2026)

funFact: New Horizons left Earth faster than any spacecraft before it: it passed the Moon’s orbit in about nine hours.
